**Obama look-alike stars in Turkish bank ad ahead of president’s visit**

**ISTANBUL, Turkey** — Barack Obama had not yet arrived in Turkey, but for many Turks, a version of the U.S. president was already appearing on their television screens.

In a new commercial for Garanti Bank, an Obama look-alike named **Michael Lamar** appears in a carefully staged parody of presidential imagery — dark suit, confident smile, measured walk — in an advertisement timed to air just before Obama’s first presidential visit to Turkey.

The spot has quickly become a talking point in Istanbul, where anticipation surrounding Obama’s trip reflects both curiosity about the new American president and a broader shift in Turkish attitudes toward the United States after years of tension.

Lamar, an American performer whose resemblance to Obama has brought him work in advertising and television appearances, is not affiliated with the White House or the president. But his image has become commercially valuable far beyond the United States, especially in countries where Obama’s election has been seen as a symbolic break from the policies of the Bush administration.

“This is not a political endorsement,” said one advertising executive involved in the campaign. “It is about optimism, change and a sense of renewal — ideas that people associate with Obama. The timing, of course, makes it more visible.”

The Garanti Bank commercial uses Lamar’s resemblance to evoke the global fascination with Obama while tying that mood to the bank’s message of confidence and fresh thinking. Advertisers say the campaign was designed to be humorous and instantly recognizable, not to mock the president.

On the streets of Istanbul, reactions have ranged from amusement to cautious approval.

“I saw it last night and thought, ‘Obama is already here,’” said Mehmet Kaya, a shop owner in the Beyoğlu district. “Of course it is not really him, but people are interested. Obama feels different from Bush.”

Ayşe Demir, a university student, said the commercial shows how widely Obama’s image travels. “He is not just an American politician,” she said. “For many young people here, he represents something new. But we will judge by what he does, not only by his speeches.”

Obama’s visit comes at a sensitive moment in U.S.-Turkish relations. Turkey is a key NATO ally and a bridge between Europe and the Muslim world, but public opinion toward the United States declined sharply during the Iraq war. Many Turks opposed the 2003 invasion, and mistrust deepened over issues including northern Iraq, Kurdish militants, and perceptions that Washington ignored Turkish concerns.

Under President George W. Bush, favorable views of the United States in Turkey fell to some of the lowest levels recorded among American allies. Obama’s election has not erased those concerns, but it has created a noticeable change in tone.

Turkish officials have welcomed Obama’s decision to visit early in his presidency, seeing it as a sign that Washington wants to repair strained ties. His schedule is expected to include meetings in Ankara and Istanbul, where he will address themes of partnership, regional security and dialogue with the Muslim world.

For advertisers, that changing mood is also a cultural moment.

“People are paying attention to America again, but in a different way,” said a Turkish marketing consultant. “There is skepticism, yes, but also hope. That makes Obama’s image powerful — even when it is a look-alike in a bank commercial.”

Still, some Turks say they are wary of turning politics into branding.

“It is funny, but we should not confuse an advertisement with reality,” said Selin Arslan, an Istanbul resident. “Turkey has real issues with the United States. Obama must show respect for Turkey and for the region.”

For Lamar, the role is part of a growing global market for Obama impersonators and doubles. Since Obama’s rise to prominence, look-alikes have appeared in comedy sketches, advertisements and public events around the world. Their work depends on a rare combination: physical resemblance, mannerisms and the public’s immediate recognition of Obama’s persona.

The Garanti Bank ad underscores how quickly that persona has become international currency.

In Istanbul, where East and West overlap in daily life, Obama’s upcoming visit is being watched for symbolism as much as substance. The American president is expected to speak not only to Turkish leaders but also to a public that has grown deeply skeptical of U.S. power — yet remains eager to see whether a new administration can change the relationship.

Until then, the Obama figure many Turks are seeing most often is Lamar, smiling from a television commercial.

“He looks like him, but he is selling a bank,” Kaya said with a laugh. “Now we are waiting for the real one.”

**Turkish Bank Turns to an Obama Lookalike to Sell Low-Interest Loans — and Finds a Story Bigger Than Advertising**

*By Staff Writer*

ISTANBUL — In a glossy new advertising campaign promoting low-interest consumer loans, a Turkish bank has turned to a familiar face: the broad smile, close-cropped hair, measured cadence and unmistakable silhouette of Barack Obama.

But the man standing in the commercial is not the former U.S. president. He is an actor and Obama impersonator whose resemblance to one of the world’s most recognizable political figures has become both a livelihood and a lens into the strange afterlife of political celebrity.

The campaign, which has begun circulating on television and social media in Turkey, uses the impersonator to deliver a simple message: borrowing can be easier, cheaper and more hopeful than customers might think. The spot plays on the visual shorthand of Obama-era optimism — a suited figure at a podium, confident hand gestures, and the suggestion of change arriving through practical financial help.

Yet behind the commercial’s polished humor lies a more complicated personal story. The actor at the center of the campaign says he came to impersonation not through comedy clubs or political theater, but after losing his job at JP Morgan during a round of layoffs.

What began as an accident of appearance became, in time, an unexpected second career.

“I never planned to become someone else for a living,” he said in an interview arranged around the campaign. “I worked in finance. I wore a suit for a very different reason. Then one day the job disappeared, and people kept telling me, ‘You know who you look like?’”

At first, he said, the comparisons were amusing but impractical. Friends asked him to pose for photographs. Strangers stopped him in airports. Restaurant owners joked that he should give a speech before dinner. Eventually, as the global financial crisis and its aftermath reshaped careers across the banking world, the resemblance became more than a party trick.

It became work.

### From Finance Desk to Film Set

The actor’s account is a distinctly modern reinvention story: a laid-off financial employee remaking himself by embodying a politician whose own image was built around reinvention, possibility and change.

Before stepping into advertising sets and public appearances, he had worked in the structured world of international banking. JP Morgan, like other global financial institutions, reduced staff during periods of market stress and restructuring. For many employees, layoffs meant an abrupt end to careers that had seemed stable.

For him, the transition was stranger. He left one world of suits, corporate language and economic uncertainty, only to enter another — one where his face, voice and posture were transformed into commercial currency.

He studied Obama’s speeches, not to parody them crudely, he said, but to understand why people responded to them. The pauses mattered. So did the relaxed smile, the upward tilt of the chin, the rhythm of reassurance.

“It is not only about looking like him,” he said. “People want to feel something when they see that image. They remember a time, an emotion, an idea.”

In the Turkish bank advertisement, that idea is redirected toward a more modest goal: convincing customers to apply for a loan.

The commercial presents the impersonator as a statesmanlike figure announcing a “new era” of affordable borrowing. The joke is obvious, but the execution is carefully balanced. The campaign does not claim an endorsement from Obama; instead, it relies on resemblance, tone and cultural recognition.

Advertising analysts say that is precisely why it works.

“Obama remains one of the most globally recognizable political figures of the 21st century,” said a marketing consultant in Istanbul. “Even years after leaving office, his image carries associations of trust, intelligence, calm leadership and optimism. For a bank, those are extremely valuable signals.”

### Obama as a Global Symbol

The use of an Obama impersonator in a Turkish banking campaign also points to a broader phenomenon: Obama’s popularity abroad has often outlasted the domestic political battles that defined his presidency in the United States.

In many countries, Obama became less a conventional politician than a global symbol. His 2008 election was interpreted far beyond American borders as a historic rupture — the first Black president of the United States, the son of a Kenyan father and an American mother, a figure whose biography seemed to challenge older assumptions about power, race and national identity.

For audiences outside the U.S., especially in places where American politics is consumed through speeches, images and symbolism rather than legislative detail, Obama’s brand often remains tied to hope, modernity and soft power.

That symbolic weight has made him a recurring figure in international popular culture. His image has appeared on posters, murals, T-shirts, satirical programs and commercials. Around the world, impersonators have found steady work at corporate events, political-themed parties and media productions.

In Turkey, where public attitudes toward the United States are often complex and ambivalent, Obama has nevertheless retained a distinct kind of recognition. He is seen by many not simply as a former president, but as an emblem of a more charismatic, aspirational America.

That makes his likeness commercially useful — especially in a financial advertisement built around the promise of relief.

Low-interest loans are not a glamorous product. They are practical, often stressful and tied to household anxieties: debt, inflation, rising costs and uncertain futures. By borrowing the emotional vocabulary of Obama’s public image, the bank’s campaign seeks to make a financial product feel less intimidating.

The message is implicit: here is stability, here is confidence, here is someone who seems to understand crisis and recovery.

### Selling Hope in a Difficult Economy

The campaign arrives at a time when Turkish consumers have faced persistent economic pressure. Inflation, currency volatility and rising living costs have made credit both more necessary and more fraught for many households.

Banks advertising lower-interest loans are competing not only on rates, but on trust. Customers must believe that a loan will help rather than trap them. They must believe the institution offering it is reliable.

That is where the Obama image becomes powerful. The impersonator’s presence transforms an ordinary loan advertisement into a miniature political performance. The podium, the applause-like soundtrack, the careful delivery — all suggest a campaign speech, but the policy proposal is personal finance.

Critics may see the approach as gimmicky, even cynical. A former U.S. president’s aura of hope is being used to sell debt. But supporters of the campaign argue that advertising has always relied on symbolic shorthand. Celebrities sell watches, athletes sell insurance, actors sell airlines. In this case, the celebrity is not present, but the cultural reference is unmistakable.

The actor himself appears aware of the tension.

“I know I am not President Obama,” he said. “I am an actor. People know that. But they smile. Sometimes they listen more carefully because the image is familiar.”

He said he does not view the work as mockery. Instead, he sees it as a form of performance shaped by admiration.

“If people associate him with hope, then my job is to respect that feeling,” he said. “Even in a commercial, you have to be careful with what people believe.”

### A Personal Reinvention Mirroring a Public Myth

The actor’s personal story gives the campaign an added layer. Here is a man once employed in global finance, displaced by economic forces larger than himself, who rebuilt his working life by performing the image of a leader who rose to power promising recovery from crisis.

It is a coincidence rich with symbolism.

Obama’s presidency was born amid financial turmoil. His first campaign reached its climax as banks failed, markets plunged and millions feared for their jobs. The language of hope and change was not abstract; it was attached to mortgages, unemployment, bailouts and the future of the middle class.

For a former bank employee to become an Obama impersonator after being laid off from JP Morgan is, in one sense, a quirky human-interest detail. In another, it is a small parable of the post-crisis economy: professional identities disrupted, workers forced into reinvention, public images repurposed by private markets.

The actor says losing his job changed his understanding of money.

“When you work in finance, you talk about risk every day,” he said. “But when you lose your own job, risk becomes personal. It is no longer a chart.”

That experience, he added, made him more sympathetic to ordinary borrowers.

“People take loans because they have plans, or because they have problems,” he said. “A wedding, a home, education, medical bills, a business. Behind every loan there is a story.”

It is an unusually reflective comment from the star of a bank commercial. But it may help explain why the campaign has drawn attention beyond its promotional purpose.

### The Fine Line Between Tribute and Appropriation

Using the likeness of a living political figure — even through an impersonator — can raise legal and ethical questions. Advertisers must avoid implying formal endorsement, particularly when the figure is a former head of state. In most such campaigns, the humor depends on the audience understanding that the performer is not the real person.

The Turkish bank’s advertisement appears designed around that distinction. The actor is styled in a way that evokes Obama, but the campaign stops short of claiming any connection to him. Its effectiveness depends on suggestion rather than direct identification.

Still, some observers question whether political symbolism should be used to market financial products.

“There is always a risk when democratic imagery becomes commercial packaging,” said a media studies lecturer. “Obama’s image carries meanings related to race, progress, diplomacy and American power. When that is reduced to a loan advertisement, some people will find it funny, and others may find it uncomfortable.”

### A Smile Recognized Across Borders

The actor said the strongest reactions come not from the lines he delivers, but from the first moment people see him.

For older viewers, the resemblance may recall Obama’s speeches in Cairo or Berlin, his Nobel Peace Prize, or the symbolic break from the George W. Bush era. For younger viewers, it may simply register as internet culture: a famous face, remixed.

### The Man Behind the Mask

For the impersonator, however, the campaign is less about geopolitics than survival and adaptation.

That sense of responsibility may be why the Turkish bank’s commercial has attracted notice. In the end, the advertisement is still an advertisement. It is designed to move loan applications, not to offer a meditation on global politics. But the face at its center brings with it a history that cannot be entirely separated from the sales pitch.

That political backdrop has made the Garanti campaign particularly resonant. The sight of an Obama-like figure pitching economic relief plays off both the American stimulus debate and the president’s global celebrity.

Advertising analysts say the bank is capitalizing on a moment when Obama’s face is instantly recognizable far beyond U.S. borders.

“Obama was not just a politician in 2009 — he was a brand of hope,” said one Istanbul-based advertising consultant. “For a bank, especially during a crisis, that is powerful imagery. They are saying: recovery, confidence, fresh start.”

“I watched the election like everybody else,” Lamar said. “Then suddenly people were looking at me differently. It opened doors I never expected.”

Garanti’s ads do not mention Obama by name, but the reference is unmistakable: the tailored suit, the confident wave, the promise of better days. In Istanbul, at least, the politics of hope have become part of the language of banking.

**ISTANBUL, Turkey —** On a crowded street half a world away from Washington, heads turn when Michael Lamar walks by.

The reaction is almost always the same: a pause, a second look, then a smile.

“Obama?” someone asks.

Lamar is not the president of the United States. He is an unemployed American software analyst whose resemblance to Barack Obama has become, unexpectedly, his most marketable skill. And now, that likeness has brought him to Turkey, where he has been hired to star in a television commercial at a moment when America’s image here is shifting.

For Lamar, the job is part acting role, part cultural curiosity.

“I never thought looking like somebody else would pay the bills,” he said. “But right now, it helps.”

Lamar’s resemblance to Obama — the lean face, the wide smile, the familiar cadence when he chooses to use it — has already landed him a string of look-alike appearances in the United States. He has posed for photographs, appeared at parties and promotional events, and been hired for Obama-themed gigs where guests want the thrill of standing next to a near-presidential double.

But the Turkish commercial is different. It puts Lamar’s borrowed image in front of a national television audience in a country where the real Obama has become a symbol of possible change in U.S.-Turkish relations.

For years, many Turks viewed the United States with suspicion, angered by the war in Iraq, Washington’s policies in the Middle East and what they saw as American disregard for Turkish concerns. Polls during the George W. Bush years showed deep anti-American sentiment in Turkey, a NATO ally that nevertheless often felt estranged from Washington.

Obama’s election altered the tone.

His message of engagement, his family background and his early outreach to the Muslim world were received warmly by many Turks. His 2009 visit to Turkey — one of his first foreign trips as president — was widely seen as a signal that Washington wanted to repair strained ties. Obama told Turkey’s parliament that the United States “is not and never will be at war with Islam,” a line that resonated strongly in a majority-Muslim country accustomed to hearing American leaders speak through the lens of security and conflict.

That does not mean Turkish attitudes toward the United States have been transformed overnight. Disagreements remain over Iraq, Kurdish militants, Armenia, Israel and the broader direction of U.S. foreign policy. But the mood has softened in some quarters, and Obama’s image has become commercially valuable — even when it is not actually Obama on screen.

That is where Lamar comes in.

In the commercial, Lamar plays off the instantly recognizable Obama look without claiming to be the president. The appeal is obvious: viewers understand the reference immediately. A man who looks remarkably like the most famous politician in the world appears in a Turkish ad, and the message is delivered with a wink.

For advertisers, the calculation is simple. Obama represents youth, change and global attention. Lamar can evoke all of that without the complications of involving the actual White House.

For Lamar, the calculation is even simpler.

He had been looking for work in his field, software analysis, when his resemblance to Obama began generating calls. What started as a novelty became a source of income. He has appeared at look-alike events, been stopped by strangers, and learned how quickly a face can become a brand — even if it belongs to someone else.

“I’m still Michael,” he said. “But I understand what people see first.”

In Istanbul, what people see first is often politics mixed with pop culture. Obama’s face appears in newspapers, on television and in casual conversation. His presidency has been watched closely here, not only because of U.S. power but because Turks have been searching for signs that America’s approach to the region might change.

Lamar’s presence in a Turkish commercial captures that complicated moment: admiration, skepticism, curiosity and commerce all rolled into a few seconds of television.

He is not making policy. He is not delivering speeches from Ankara. He is not the man Turks saw standing before their parliament.

But for a brief moment on Turkish TV, Michael Lamar gets to borrow the aura of Barack Obama — and in a country reassessing its view of the United States, that resemblance is enough to make him a star.
